title: Practice, one small nudge at a time
blurb: How the model learns: it tries a question, is shown the right answer, and each learned setting moves a tiny bit. This part covers the practice loop, the data, the fairness rules and the cost.

scenes.heading: The recipe: how each nudge is made

caption.text: AdamW is the nudging rule. The learning rate is how big a nudge may be.
It starts small, peaks at 1e-3 after a 300-update warm-up, then falls to 10% of the peak.
Sums run in short numbers (bf16), rows come shuffled, and the start is random.

scenes.heading: Fair practice: three rules

caption.text: Rule 1: no answer is cut short. A longer answer is counted, and any count above 0 fails the pass mark.
Rule 2: exam questions are kept apart: 6,040 rows are never used in practice, though question styles can repeat.
Rule 3: web text is scanned against exam sets. A last scan, on sealed sets, was pending Oct 9; the 3M runs began before it.

scenes.heading: Time: our model versus the plain model

caption.text: Ours did 24,000 updates on the project's PC: 1.02 updates a second, 6.51 hours.
The plain model, a standard transformer of about the same size, also did 24,000 updates: 2.8 a second, 2.38 hours.
Our division: 6.51 ÷ 2.38, about 2.7 times longer. Our other 3M copy took 16.3 hours; a memory spill is the suggested cause.
A plan, not a result: the 100M run (about 100 million numbers) is estimated at 3 to 5 weeks on this PC.

scenes.heading: Why the thinker is harder to train

caption.text: The same blocks run every round, so the lesson from a wrong answer must travel back through all of them.
To save memory, training redoes some work instead of storing it: about a third more compute (plan estimate).
Depth has a known cost: on one old probe, 16 rounds cost 1.2 to 1.9 points. At 100 million numbers it is an open risk.
